'''Thomas Gerald Room''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] [[Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science|FAA]] (10 November 1902 – 2 April 1986) was an [[Australians|Australian]] [[mathematician]] who is best known for [[Room square]]s. He was a Foundation [[Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science]].<ref name="hw">
{{Cite journal | last1 = Hirschfeld | first1 = J. W. P. | last2 = Wall | first2 = G. E. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1987.0020  | doi-access = free| title = Thomas Gerald Room. 10 November 1902 – 2 April 1986 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 33 | pages = 575–601 | year = 1987| jstor = 769963 | s2cid = 73328766 }}. Also published in ''Historical Records of Australian Science'' '''7''' (1): 109–122, {{doi|10.1071/HR9870710109}}. An abridged version is [http://www.asap.unimelb.edu.au/bsparcs/aasmemoirs/room.htm online at the web site of the Australian Academy of Science].</ref><ref name=ADB>
{{cite Australian Dictionary of Biography |author= John Mack |id2=room-thomas-gerald-14198 |title= Room, Thomas Gerald (1902–1986) }} First published in ''Australian Dictionary of Biography'', Volume 18, (MUP), 2012.</ref>  Room was born in London and educated at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] he moved to Sydney, Australia, in 1935.  During the Second World War he worked for the Australian government to decrypt coded Japanese communications.  After the war Room became dean of the faculty of science at the [[University of Sydney]] and later worked in the US and England.

==Biography==
Thomas Room was born on 10 November 1902, near [[London]], [[England]]. He studied mathematics in [[St John's College, Cambridge]], and was a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in 1923. He continued at Cambridge as a graduate student, and was elected as a fellow in 1925, but instead took a position at the [[University of Liverpool]]. He returned to Cambridge in 1927, at which time he completed his PhD, with a thesis supervised by [[H. F. Baker]].<ref>Hirschfeld, J. W. P.; Wall, G. E. (1987). "Thomas Gerald Room. 10 November 1902 – 2 April 1986", ''Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society'' 33: 574. doi:10.1098/rsbm.1987.0020. JSTOR 769963.. Also published in ''Historical Records of Australian Science'' 7 (1): 109–122, doi:10.1071/HR9870710109. An abridged version is online at the web site of the Australian Academy of Science.</ref><ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|name=Thomas Gerald Room|id=18506}}</ref> Room remained at Cambridge until 1935, when he moved to the [[University of Sydney]], where he accepted the position of Chair of the Mathematics Department, a position he held until his retirement in 1968.<ref>"The University. Chair of Mathematics. Professor T. G. Room", ''The Sydney Morning Herald'', 21 December 1934.</ref>

During [[World War II]] he worked for the Australian government, helping to [[decrypt]] Japanese communications. In January 1940, with the encouragement of the Australian Army, he, together with some colleagues at the University of Sydney, began to study Japanese codes. The others were the mathematician Richard Lyons and the classicists [[Arthur Dale Trendall]] and [[Athanasius Treweek]]. By this time Room had already begun learning Japanese under Margaret Ethel Lake (1883-?) at the University of Sydney. In May 1941 Room and Treweek attended a meeting at the Victoria Barracks in Melbourne with the Director of Naval Intelligence of the [[Royal Australian Navy]], several Australian Army intelligence officers and [[Eric Nave]], an expert Japanese cryptographer with the Royal Australian Navy. As a result, it was agreed that Room's group, with the agreement of the University of Sydney, would move in August 1941 to work under Nave at the Special Intelligence Bureau in Melbourne. On 1 September 1941, Room was sent to the [[Far East Combined Bureau]] in Singapore to study the codebreaking techniques used there. After the outbreak of war they were working for [[FRUMEL]] (Fleet Radio Unit Melbourne), a joint American-Australian intelligence unit, but when Lieutenant Rudolph Fabian took over command of FRUMEL and particularly when, in October 1942, FRUMEL was placed under direct control of the US Navy, civilians such as the member of Room's group were found surplus to requirements and returned to their academic posts.<ref>Peter Kornicki, ''Eavesdropping on the Emperor: Interrogators and Codebreakers in Britain's War with Japan'' (London: Hurst & Co., 2021),  pp. 209-211, 216-7.</ref><ref>Peter Donovan,  and John Mack, ‘Sydney University, T. G. Room and codebreaking in WW II’, ''Australian mathematical society gazette'' 29 (2002): 76-85, 141-8.</ref>

After the war, Room served as dean of the faculty of science at the University of Sydney from 1952 to 1956 and again from 1960 to 1965.<ref>Hirschfeld, J. W. P.; Wall, G. E. (1987), "Thomas Gerald Room. 10 November 1902 – 2 April 1986". ''Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society'' 33: 574. doi:10.1098/rsbm.1987.0020. JSTOR 769963. Also published in ''Historical Records of Australian Science'' 7 (1): 109–122, doi:10.1071/HR9870710109. An abridged version is online at the web site of the Australian Academy of Science.</ref> He also held visiting positions at the [[University of Washington]] in 1948, and the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] and [[Princeton University]] in 1957.<ref name="Hirschfeld, J. W. P. 1987">Hirschfeld, J. W. P.; Wall, G. E. (1987). "Thomas Gerald Room. 10 November 1902 – 2 April 1986". ''Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society'' 33: 574. doi:10.1098/rsbm.1987.0020. JSTOR 769963.. Also published in ''Historical Records of Australian Science'' 7 (1): 109–122, doi:10.1071/HR9870710109. An abridged version is online at the web site of the Australian Academy of Science.</ref><ref>{{citation|journal=[[The New York Times]]|title=Princeton Appoints 17 Guest Professors|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1957/09/04/archives/princeton-appoints-17-guest-professors.html|date=4 September 1957}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1957/09/15/archives/institute-names-128-for-research-scholars-will-do-advanced-study-on.html|journal=[[The New York Times]]|title=Institute Names 128 For Research; Scholars Will Do Advanced Study on Historical Topics And in Mathematics|date=15 September 1957}}.</ref> He retired from Sydney in 1968 but took short-term positions afterwards at [[Westfield College]] in London and the [[Open University]] before returning to Australia in 1974. He died on 2 April 1986.

Room married Jessica Bannerman, whom he met in Sydney, in 1937; they had one son and two daughters.<ref name="Hirschfeld, J. W. P. 1987"/><ref>{{citation |title= Professor and Bride Dodge Rice |journal= [[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|url= http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article17413743?searchTerm=t.+g.+room |date=8 November 1937}}.</ref>

==Research==
Room's PhD work concerned generalizations of the Schläfli double six, a [[Configuration (geometry)|configuration]] formed by the 27 lines on a cubic [[algebraic surface]].<ref name="hw"/><ref name="mg"/>

In 1938 he published the book ''The geometry of determinantal loci'' through the [[Cambridge University Press]].<ref name="hw"/> Nearly 500 pages long, the book combines methods of [[synthetic geometry]] and [[algebraic geometry]] to study higher-dimensional generalizations of [[quartic surface]]s and [[cubic surface]]s. It describes many infinite families of [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]], and individual varieties in these families, following a unifying principle that nearly all [[Locus (mathematics)|loci]] arising in algebraic geometry can be expressed as the solution to an equation involving the [[determinant]] of an appropriate [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]].<ref name="hw"/><ref name="vs39">Review of ''The geometry of determinantal loci'' by Virgil Snyder (1939), ''Bulletin of the AMS'' '''45''': 499–501, {{doi|10.1090/S0002-9904-1939-07011-0}}.</ref>

In the postwar period, Room shifted the focus of his work to [[Clifford algebra]] and [[spinor]] [[group (mathematics)|groups]].<ref name="hw"/> Later, in the 1960s, he also began investigating [[finite geometry]], and wrote a textbook on the foundations of geometry.<ref name="hw"/>

Room invented [[Room square]]s in a brief note published in 1955.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Room | first = T. G. | journal = Mathematical Gazette | page = 307 | title = A new type of magic square | volume = 39
 | year = 1955| doi = 10.2307/3608578 | jstor = 3608578 | s2cid = 125711658 }}.</ref> A Room square is an ''n''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''n'' grid in which some of the cells are filled by sets of two of the numbers from 0 to ''n'' in such a way that each number appears once in each row or column and each two-element set occupies exactly one cell of the grid. Although Room squares had previously been studied by [[Robert Richard Anstice]],<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Anstice|title=Robert Anstice}}.</ref> Anstice's work had become forgotten and Room squares were named after Room. In his initial work on the subject, Room showed that, for a Room square to exist, ''n'' must be odd and cannot equal 3 or 5. It was later shown by W. D. Wallis in 1973 that these are necessary and sufficient conditions: every other odd value of ''n'' has an associated Room square. The nonexistence of a Room square for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5 and its existence for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;7 can both be explained in terms of configurations in [[projective geometry]].<ref name="hw"/>

Despite retiring in 1968, Room remained active mathematically for several more years, and published the book ''Miniquaternion geometry: An introduction to the study of projective planes'' in 1971 with his student Philip B. Kirkpatrick.<ref name="hw"/>

==Awards and honours==
In 1941, Room won the [[Thomas Ranken Lyle Medal]] of the Australian National Research Council and was elected as a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref name="hw"/><ref>{{citation |title=Lyle Medals Awarded |journal=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article17747686?searchTerm=lyle+medal+briggs |date=10 July 1941}}.</ref><ref>[http://www.science.org.au/awards/awards/lyle.html Thomas Ranken Lyle Medal] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101128133557/http://science.org.au/awards/awards/lyle.html |date=28 November 2010 }}, [[Australian Academy of Science]]. Retrieved 6 June 2010.</ref> He was one of the Foundation Fellows of the [[Australian Academy of Science]], chartered in 1954.<ref name="hw"/><ref name=ADB/> From 1960 to 1962, he served as president of the [[Australian Mathematical Society]] and he later became the first editor of its journal.<ref name="hw"/>

The T. G. Room award of the Mathematical Association of New South Wales, awarded to the student with the best score in the NSW [[Higher School Certificate (New South Wales)|Higher School Certificate]] Mathematics Extension 2 examination, is named in Room's honour.<ref name="hw"/><ref>[http://www.mansw.nsw.edu.au/studentservices/tgroom-award.htm The T G Room Award] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120804020113/http://www.mansw.nsw.edu.au/studentservices/tgroom-award.htm |date=4 August 2012 }}, Mathematical Association of New South Wales. Retrieved 1 June 2010.</ref>
